fields.v: Zhang, W., You, G., Tianlun, Zhao, H., Zhu, T., Wang, H., Tang, X., Dai, M., Gu, J., Dong, D., Wu, J. (2026). WebGameBench: Requirement-to-Application Evaluation for Coding Agents via Browser-Native Games. arXiv:2605.17637v2 [cs.AI], 21 May 2026
Preprint — arXiv:2605.17637v2 [cs.AI]; marked 'Preprint.', no venue stated
Baidu (all authors except You); University of Science and Technology of China (You)

Proposes an evaluation method; secondary: Compares — WebGameBench, a requirement-to-application benchmark: agents turn a frozen Structured WebGame Specification into a browser game that is deployed and judged by an LLM runtime evaluator through real browser interaction (EXCELLENT / USABLE / UNUSABLE); 14 configurations of 12 coding agents compared; evaluator validated against human gameplay review

No SDD approach. Benchmark input: Structured WebGame Specification (a PRD-style frozen requirement). Configurations (models in a unified generation environment; generation agent/harness not named): opus-4-7, opus-4-6, sonnet-4-5, gpt-5-5, gemini-3.1-pro, deepseek-v4-pro and deepseek-v4-flash (each thinking and no-thinking), kimi-k2.6, kimi-k2.5, GLM-5.1, GLM-5, hy3-xhigh. Runtime evaluator: Codex CLI 0.115.0 with gpt-5.4-agent backend, XHigh reasoning, Playwright-controlled Chrome

Structured WebGame Specification per task, fixed template: game overview, page and flow, input controls, game objects, rules and state changes, visual feedback, technical and deployment constraints, evaluable functional points / acceptance criteria (called a PRD in the engineering pipeline). Derived metadata: B-S-T functional-point annotation and D-level difficulty label. Output: source artifact (.zip) and deployed URL; evaluator produces a structured evaluation report

Construction: seed discovery from public game portals and user requests -> seed abstraction -> specification synthesis by an LLM prompt (frozen) -> functional-point and difficulty annotation -> feasibility filtering and coverage selection. Evaluation: agent generation (one attempt; plan, code, run, debug, self-check loop in a standard workspace) -> build, serve, expose URL -> runtime evaluation (smoke interaction, checks derived from spec, user-level actions, evidence, label)

None in the generation loop. Human gameplay review of a 43-artifact subset by five annotators (two independent tests per artifact) and two senior experts inspecting disagreements, used to validate the evaluator
Specification format only (structured requirement document as the sole agent input; no SDD workflow)
Not classifiable (authors call the input a 'frozen Structured WebGame Specification', a 'task contract', 'sometimes called a PRD'; no SDD terms)
New project (build a browser-native game from the specification in a common workspace template)
111 tasks; 19-80 atomic functional points per task (mean 36.20, median 33; 4,018 total); D-levels D1 12, D2 21, D3 71, D4 7; 82.9% of tasks structural scale S1/S2, 72.1% logical depth L3/L4

Browser-native games in seven gameplay families (Puzzle/Matching, Action/Arcade/Platform, Shooting/Combat, Racing/Sports/Skill, Strategy/Simulation/Management, Casual/Reaction/Idle, Board/Card/Local Multiplayer); web stack React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind, shadcn/ui
N/A (autonomous agents; human reviewers only for evaluator validation)

Not compared: dollar cost explicitly not reported; generation and evaluation turn counts given as compute-effort proxy for three sampled configurations only (generation mean about 20-24 turns, evaluation about 31-35). 2-hour timeout per sample

Three-way runtime label per artifact (EXCELLENT, USABLE, UNUSABLE); Usable rate Ruse (EXCELLENT or USABLE over valid samples); Excellent rate Rexc; coverage (share of attempts with a valid label); usable/valid counts by D-level
None
None

Evaluator-human agreement (accuracy and macro-F1 on Ruse label and on three-way labels, by evaluator reasoning setting); D-level annotation stability (about 90% single-request agreement with majority labels); qualitative runtime case studies

Automatic: LLM-agent runtime evaluator (Codex CLI 0.115.0, gpt-5.4-agent, XHigh) interacting with the deployed game through Playwright, one rollout per artifact, judgement grounded in observable behaviour; build/install/serving failures counted as UNUSABLE. Manual: human gameplay review of 43 artifacts to validate the evaluator

Benchmark WebGameBench, 111 tasks, one generation attempt each (Table 1). Values: coverage / Excellent rate / Usable rate. Success criterion: per artifact, USABLE = playable main path, EXCELLENT = complete and stable satisfaction of main requirements (label thresholds defined by the authors); no criterion stated for a configuration as a whole. (1) opus-4-7: 93.7% / 20.2% / 76.9%. (2) opus-4-6: 90.1% / 19.0% / 73.0%. (3) gpt-5-5: 99.1% / 16.4% / 63.6%. (4) gemini-3.1-pro: 96.4% / 15.9% / 63.6%. (5) deepseek-v4-flash-thinking: 99.1% / 13.6% / 62.7%. (6) deepseek-v4-pro-thinking: 100.0% / 12.6% / 62.2%. (7) kimi-k2.6: 94.6% / 16.2% / 61.0%. (8) deepseek-v4-flash-nothinking: 97.3% / 14.8% / 59.3%. (9) GLM-5.1: 97.3% / 12.0% / 52.8%. (10) GLM-5: 99.1% / 10.9% / 48.2%. (11) sonnet-4-5: 91.9% / 7.8% / 47.1%. (12) deepseek-v4-pro-nothinking: 100.0% / 16.2% / 44.1%. (13) hy3-xhigh: 95.5% / 6.6% / 41.5%. (14) kimi-k2.5: 96.4% / 8.4% / 38.3%. Agent/harness for all: not stated (unified generation environment). Quality verdict and cost verdict for every configuration: no criterion stated by the authors

Tasks: 111 frozen game specifications. Configurations: 14 (12 agents; DeepSeek-V4 Pro and Flash each with and without thinking). Baseline: none. Held constant: specifications, workspace template, tool interface, execution budget (2 h), deployment protocol, evaluator and evaluation prompt. Model reasoning settings vary by configuration. Acceptance: LLM runtime evaluator against the specification, validated on a human-reviewed subset. Repetitions: one generation attempt and one evaluation rollout per task. Human intervention: none during generation; evaluator gives no feedback to the agent

opus-4-7 best (Usable 76.9%, Excellent 20.2%), then opus-4-6 (73.0%, 19.0%); middle band around 60%; lowest 38.3%-52.8%. Excellent rate at most 20.2% and mostly below 17%: crossing the playable threshold is far easier than full requirement satisfaction. Pooled usable rate by D-level: D1 73.7%, D2 76.1%, D3 52.1%, D4 12.6%. Evaluator-human agreement on Ruse rises with evaluator reasoning (Medium 66.7% acc / 65.9% F1, High 82.1% / 80.8%, XHigh 85.0% / 82.9%); three-way agreement under XHigh 50.0% / 50.5% (12 human-EXCELLENT downgraded to USABLE). No significance tests

Partly. Authors report clear, interpretable separation of configurations and D-level directionally aligned with usable rate; evaluator agrees reasonably with humans on the Usable criterion but exact three-way labelling (Excellent boundary) is weak, so Excellent-rate analysis still needs human review. Repeatability not assessed (single attempt and rollout)

Runtime evaluator is not a substitute for human review; exact three-way labelling limited. Results are evidence about browser-accessible interactive artifacts, not general software-engineering competence. Specifications come from fixed templates and filtering; constructed preconditions cannot exhaust long-horizon, randomized or multi-session behaviour. Benchmark positioned as a diagnostic complement to human review, not a certification of application quality

Values from Table 1 (p. 7) and Figure 4 (p. 8). Human-review set stated as 43 artifacts, but Figure 4 heatmaps sum to 39 (Medium, High) and 40 (XHigh) samples. Pilot (Figure 1, opus-4-6 on games: 77.9% usable, 21.5% excellent) differs from Table 1 (73.0%, 19.0%); the pilot is stated to be separate. The generation agent/harness and tool interface are not named. The evaluator uses an OpenAI model (gpt-5.4) while GPT-5.5 is among the evaluated configurations; possible self-preference not discussed. Specifications and D-levels produced with LLM prompts (model not stated). No data or code release link given; no pre-registration. Programming language: TypeScript (React/Vite stack)
Yes (1): aim (requirement-to-application evaluation) and three contributions clearly stated
Partly (0.5): specification template, annotation rubric and evaluator protocol described; generation agent, tool interface and workspace not specified and materials not released
Partly (0.5): model names and some reasoning settings given and evaluator version stated (Codex CLI 0.115.0); generation harness not identified
Partly (0.5): corpus described (111 tasks, families, difficulty, functional points) and template given; tasks not published and no availability statement
Partly (0.5): LLM-agent runtime evaluator against the specification, validated on a human-reviewed subset (85.0% agreement on Usable, 50.0% on three-way labels)

rev.why: Effectiveness is judged by an LLM-agent runtime evaluator against the frozen specification, not by fixed acceptance tests; it is validated on a 43-artifact human-review subset (85.0% agreement on Usable, 50.0% on three-way labels). Partly is defensible, but a reader could give Yes (independent of the authors, checked against human review) or lower it given the weak three-way agreement.
